frictionVectors.title: EU Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains reliant on Algerian pipeline and LNG supplies, creating bargaining power but also pressure for stable pricing and expanded production. Algeria is cautious about foreign control over upstream assets.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Morocco Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Instability across the southern borders and rivalry with Morocco complicate transport, energy, and security planning. Regional competition limits infrastructure integration despite Algeria's strong state control.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting US and European financing around Angolan copper and cobalt access, while China retains major commercial and infrastructure influence. Luanda seeks to capture more value without becoming dependent on any single external bloc.

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Investment Gap
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature oil fields and capital-intensive offshore projects keep Angola dependent on foreign operators and technology. This constrains the state's ability to convert hydrocarbon wealth into broader sovereign industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border and Transit Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Political hostility with Niger has disrupted established trade routes and reduced the predictability of port-linked commerce. Benin's dependence on regional transit leaves key infrastructure exposed to decisions made by neighboring governments.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners are competing for influence around port, road, and logistics projects. Benin retains policy space, but debt exposure and concession terms will determine how much value remains under national control.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Negotiation Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is using its diamond reserves and production role to demand greater local sorting, marketing, and beneficiation from De Beers. Weak global diamond demand could nevertheless reduce negotiating leverage and fiscal receipts.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: New copper, nickel, and other mineral projects require external capital and improved rail links to regional ports. Botswana's stable institutions provide leverage, but logistics costs may limit domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Sovereignty Drive
frictionVectors.details: The junta is tightening state oversight of industrial and artisanal gold production while seeking more domestic processing and revenue capture. Insecurity, smuggling, and limited technical capacity make effective control difficult.

frictionVectors.title: Security and Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support is reshaping access to strategic sites and may trade one form of external dependence for another. Persistent militant attacks threaten mines, roads, and electricity infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-DRC Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Rwanda and instability in eastern DRC constrain Burundi’s border security and trade access. Kinshasa remains a critical partner, but deeper military involvement carries escalation risks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Strategic Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Nickel and rare-mineral development depends heavily on external finance, technology, and export infrastructure. The government is seeking greater state participation but retains limited bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Airport Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and Praia attract competing European, American, Chinese, and Gulf-linked investment. External financing improves connectivity but can narrow Cabo Verde’s room to set long-term infrastructure terms.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Resource Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and limited surveillance capacity threaten fisheries and the wider blue economy. Cabo Verde relies on external partners for maritime security, monitoring, and enforcement technology.

highlights: Oil, Gas, and Timber Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders remain important to roads, hydropower, and industrial projects, while repayment and local-content concerns limit Cameroon’s control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Gulf of Guinea Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts agricultural and transport networks, while piracy and armed crime threaten offshore energy routes and regional trade.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-Mining Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on Russian-linked security forces has helped protect the capital and selected corridors but is associated with opaque access to gold and diamond concessions. This weakens transparency and limits independent state control of resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Border and Logistics Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Conflict spillover from Sudan and insecurity along routes through Chad and Cameroon restrict exports and humanitarian access. Poor roads and reliance on neighboring transit states leave Bangui vulnerable to external pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Conflict and Refugee Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The war in Sudan is driving refugees, arms flows, and cross-border insecurity into eastern Chad. N'Djamena’s security dependence and border mobilization divert resources from civilian development.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Infrastructure and External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil revenues and export infrastructure remain central to state finances, with foreign operators and transit arrangements shaping the sector. Falling production, opaque contracts, and limited diversification constrain sovereign control over national wealth.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte and maritime sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Comoros continues to contest French control of Mayotte, while migration and maritime-security tensions complicate bilateral relations. France remains an indispensable security and economic partner despite the dispute.

frictionVectors.title: Connectivity and aid dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic infrastructure leaves the archipelago reliant on external financing, remittances, and foreign-backed telecommunications and transport projects.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper bargaining pressure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a dominant position in industrial mining, while the United States, European partners, and Gulf actors seek access to strategic minerals. Kinshasa is pursuing greater value capture but remains constrained by financing, processing gaps, and contract dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern security and regional interference
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border tensions around North and South Kivu continue to limit sovereign control over territory and mineral corridors. Regional diplomacy is competing with military and commercial interests linked to neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: State finances and export capacity remain heavily dependent on oil, leaving Brazzaville exposed to price cycles and the negotiating power of international energy companies and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, public works, and resource-linked projects have expanded connectivity but also increased dependence on external contractors and creditors. French commercial and political influence remains significant.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire has strengthened farmer pricing and sector regulation, but foreign traders and processors still capture much of the value from the world's leading cocoa supply base. Climate stress and traceability rules add pressure to domestic producers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and transport corridors attract investment from France, China, Gulf states, and regional partners. The competition supports growth but creates long-term exposure to foreign capital, operators, and strategic concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign base concentration
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti derives major revenue and diplomatic leverage from hosting American, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other foreign military facilities. The arrangement strengthens regime security while narrowing strategic autonomy and increasing exposure to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked port and logistics infrastructure is central to the economy and to Ethiopia's trade access, but debt obligations and foreign operating interests constrain national control over critical corridors.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues diplomatic and security pressure over Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, viewing unilateral Nile management as an existential threat.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and strategic assets
frictionVectors.details: IMF conditions and Gulf investment are supporting fiscal stability but increasing foreign influence over ports, real estate, and other nationally strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Declining hydrocarbon output
frictionVectors.details: Maturing oil fields and limited production diversification are weakening state revenues and increasing dependence on foreign technical operators and capital.

frictionVectors.title: Regional gas competition
frictionVectors.details: Equatorial Guinea is seeking to preserve its LNG position amid competition from Nigeria, Angola, and emerging West African gas projects.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea’s coastline is increasingly important to competing Gulf, Western, and regional security interests, raising pressure on its ports and strategic alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining exposure
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide vital revenue but leave the state dependent on foreign companies, opaque contracting, and commodity-price volatility.

frictionVectors.title: Regional infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African transport corridors, energy links, markets, and customs systems, limiting independent control over trade resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Trade-preference vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, apparel, and forestry exporters remain exposed to external market-access decisions and changing standards in South Africa, the United States, and the European Union.

highlights: Debt and port access constrain leverage

frictionVectors.title: Nile dam confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD is expanding Ethiopia’s control over electricity generation while sustaining acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan over filling, operations, and downstream guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia’s search for secure maritime access, including arrangements involving Somaliland, intersects with Somali, Egyptian, Gulf, and Turkish interests while debt restructuring limits its negotiating room.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Mining and infrastructure concessions
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is seeking greater state control and local value addition in manganese and iron-ore projects, creating tension with established foreign operators. Railway capacity and export infrastructure remain vulnerable points.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms still dominate much of Gabon's mature oil industry, limiting fiscal and technological autonomy. The government must balance contract revision against the need to preserve investment and production.

highlights: Senegal remains the essential strategic partner
Port and fisheries sovereignty under pressure

frictionVectors.title: Senegambia border and trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegalese transport corridors, markets, and security cooperation. Border closures, customs disputes, or political tensions can quickly disrupt food and fuel supplies.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign access to fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing agreements and weak monitoring raise concerns that foreign fleets capture value while reducing local fish stocks. Limited enforcement capacity constrains Banjul's control over maritime resources.

highlights: Debt repair is reshaping resource policy
Gold and lithium nationalism is rising

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental loss
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal and illegal gold mining continues to damage waterways, farmland, and state legitimacy, often involving politically connected or foreign-linked networks. Efforts to formalize production face enforcement and employment trade-offs.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Accra is seeking local processing and stronger state participation in lithium and gold value chains while managing Chinese, Western, and regional competition. Fiscal pressure increases the temptation to grant rapid concessions.

highlights: Simandou is transforming Guinea's strategic weight

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor control
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project depends on large rail, port, and power investments involving international consortia, especially Chinese-linked capital. Concession terms, local-content demands, and control of export infrastructure remain major sovereignty disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite dependence and political transition
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains heavily dependent on foreign-led bauxite extraction, with limited domestic refining and processing. The military government uses mining renegotiations to assert sovereignty while political uncertainty raises risks for operators and communities.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew export capture
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends overwhelmingly on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and the state exposed to foreign traders, price swings, and limited domestic processing. Weak regulation makes value-chain upgrading difficult.

frictionVectors.title: Port, security, and trafficking pressures
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's limited port and security capacity create openings for foreign commercial influence and illicit trafficking networks. External security and development partners remain important, but their leverage exceeds the state's institutional capacity.

highlights: Regional logistics hub under strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: External financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: Heavy debt-service obligations and reliance on IMF-linked financing constrain Nairobi's freedom over infrastructure, taxation, and state-asset decisions. Chinese, Gulf, European, and U.S. interests compete for influence in transport and energy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and Lamu remain strategically important gateways for East Africa, while neighboring corridors and foreign-backed logistics projects compete for cargo and political alignment.

highlights: Water wealth traded for development finance

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project dependency
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa generate vital revenue but leave the kingdom dependent on South African infrastructure, purchasing arrangements, and downstream demand.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and energy bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Diamond mining and renewable-energy development attract foreign capital, while limited domestic fiscal capacity reduces Lesotho's leverage over ownership, taxation, and local value addition.

highlights: Ports and mining remain externally financed

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports and rail infrastructure depend on foreign operators and cross-border logistics, limiting Liberia's control over pricing, transport access, and downstream processing.

frictionVectors.title: Port concession scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: The Freeport of Monrovia and related logistics assets remain focal points for competing foreign commercial and strategic interests. Concession terms and local employment are politically sensitive.

highlights: Foreign security patrons shape infrastructure access

frictionVectors.title: Oil blockade and governance rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Competing authorities and armed networks can disrupt production, export terminals, and budget transfers, weakening the National Oil Corporation's ability to act as a unified sovereign instrument.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and commercial influence
frictionVectors.details: External powers and private security actors retain influence over bases, ports, energy projects, and political factions. This gives outside stakeholders leverage over Libya's strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and cobalt dependency
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects rely heavily on foreign capital, technology, and export markets, leaving Madagascar exposed to commodity cycles and limited domestic processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Port and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Mining exports depend on specialized ports and fragile power systems, creating leverage for foreign operators and complicating the state's ability to enforce local-content and environmental obligations.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL DEBT AND POLICY CONDITIONALITY
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF support are constraining fiscal autonomy, while creditors and development partners retain significant influence over economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND POWER INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking greater state value from uranium and rare-earth projects, but foreign capital, weak transmission capacity, and chronic electricity shortages limit sovereign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SECTOR RENEGOTIATION
frictionVectors.details: The military government is pressing foreign mining companies for larger state participation and revenues, raising tensions with established operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has displaced Western influence but has not resolved insurgency, while opaque security arrangements complicate long-term sovereignty over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: GTA GAS PROJECT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and international operators is strengthening state revenues, but production, export infrastructure, and technical expertise remain externally dependent.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE LOGISTICS
frictionVectors.details: Mauritania's mining economy remains exposed to foreign demand, rail infrastructure constraints, and Chinese and European commercial influence over transport and commodity markets.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS IMPLEMENTATION RISKS
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty settlement over the Chagos Archipelago and Diego Garcia remains strategically sensitive, with future basing, access, and financial arrangements requiring careful management among Mauritius, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCIAL EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional control, but its offshore finance, tourism, and shipping sectors remain vulnerable to regulatory pressure and external market shocks.

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is using phosphate, fisheries, ports, and renewable-energy development in Western Sahara to consolidate control, while facing legal and diplomatic challenges from Algeria and the Polisario Front.

frictionVectors.title: WATER AND ENERGY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Desalination and renewable projects are improving resilience, but drought, imported energy inputs, and dependence on foreign technology and capital remain strategic vulnerabilities.

highlights: LNG Restart Meets Cabo Delgado Risk

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant attacks continue to threaten LNG infrastructure and constrain state access in the north. Mozambique remains reliant on foreign security assistance, including Rwandan support, to protect strategic projects.

frictionVectors.title: Gas Sovereignty Gap
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies and lenders retain decisive influence over project timelines, financing, and revenue structures. Delayed production limits near-term public benefits despite the scale of Mozambique's reserves.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Major offshore discoveries are attracting international operators and could transform state revenues, but Namibia must negotiate stronger local participation and fiscal terms before production begins.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects depend on foreign capital, export infrastructure, and overseas demand. Weak domestic industrial capacity risks leaving Namibia primarily as an energy exporter rather than an owner of downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking greater control over uranium, gold, and oil assets while distancing itself from French and Western partners. Contract uncertainty and diplomatic pressure could reduce investment and technical support.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Withdrawal of Western forces and closer alignment with Russia and regional junta governments have altered security access around major transport and mining routes. Insurgent activity continues to threaten infrastructure and state revenue collection.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Delta Militancy
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, sabotage, and insecurity continue to weaken federal control over oil production and reduce public revenue. International operators retain major technical and financial leverage despite divestment and reform efforts.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Refining, gas-processing, rail, and power expansion relies heavily on private capital and foreign equipment. New domestic capacity may improve sovereignty, but financing costs and regulatory uncertainty remain substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Networks
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security influence and alleged support for M23 continue to attract international scrutiny over access to eastern Congo's minerals. Diplomatic pressure and possible sanctions threaten Kigali's regional economic model.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong administrative control but depends on external aid, concessional finance, and foreign investment for infrastructure and growth. Western political conditionality is rising as regional tensions persist.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Exploration Dependence
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe remains reliant on foreign oil companies and licensing partners to assess its offshore blocks. Unproven reserves have generated political expectations without yet delivering meaningful sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Port, aviation, and maritime-security needs leave the archipelago dependent on external financing and partnerships, creating exposure to competing Portuguese, Chinese, and Gulf interests.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil and gas production is strengthening Senegal's bargaining position, but pressure to revise contracts and increase local participation could unsettle investors and delay fiscal benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Constraints
frictionVectors.details: High financing needs limit Dakar's room to pursue an independent development model. Chinese, Gulf, European, and multilateral funding remain important to transport and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Fisheries
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on foreign fleets and external markets for much of its fisheries income, creating persistent concerns over licensing value, enforcement capacity, and sustainable control of marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: Port access, maritime surveillance, and security cooperation attract interest from India, China, France, and other partners. Victoria must balance these relationships while protecting its non-aligned posture.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mineral Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led mining remains central to exports and fiscal prospects, but weak local processing and limited bargaining capacity constrain domestic value capture. Commodity-price volatility amplifies sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Freetown's port and logistics infrastructure require external capital, exposing the country to competition among Chinese, Gulf, and Western-linked investors. Infrastructure deals can improve capacity while reducing long-term policy flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Somalia remains dependent on international partners and regional forces for counterinsurgency, training, and logistics as it seeks to assume greater control over national security. This dependence limits strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: Competing Turkish, Gulf, Ethiopian, and other interests in ports and maritime access intersect with disputes over Somaliland and Somalia's territorial authority. Offshore hydrocarbons and fisheries add further incentives for external involvement.

highlights: Grid recovery and port reforms advance unevenly
Critical-minerals diplomacy balances China, the US and EU

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND LOGISTICS BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability is improving, but Eskom finances, transmission constraints and chronic rail and port inefficiencies still limit sovereign control over coal, manganese and platinum exports.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL-MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Pretoria is seeking local beneficiation and diversified partnerships while competing external powers pursue preferential access to strategic minerals and battery supply chains.

highlights: Oil revenues remain hostage to regional instability
Peace implementation is stalled and externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on export infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving its principal revenue stream vulnerable to war damage, political leverage and competing regional interests.

frictionVectors.title: OIL-SECTOR RENT SEEKING
frictionVectors.details: Production and revenue management remain opaque, while armed and political elites compete for control of fields, contracts and transport corridors with limited public benefit.

highlights: Civil war fragments control of gold and transport corridors
External sponsors intensify a proxy-shaped conflict

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Gold-producing areas and informal export networks finance rival armed actors, with foreign traders and regional intermediaries gaining leverage over Sudan's mineral wealth.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND RED SEA COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and prospective Red Sea access has become strategically important to outside powers, while conflict threatens national infrastructure and customs revenues.

highlights: Resource nationalism is paired with selective foreign investment
Ports and gas corridors become regional power assets

frictionVectors.title: LNG AND FISCAL SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over large-scale gas development continue to test Tanzania's demands for domestic value capture against investor requirements and external energy interests.

frictionVectors.title: PORT CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam and proposed rail and logistics links are drawing Gulf, Chinese and Western attention, raising concerns over long-term concessions and strategic dependence.

highlights: Lomé consolidates its role as a Gulf of Guinea trade hub
Northern insecurity pressures a tightly managed state

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRANSIT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Togo retains formal control of Lomé's strategic infrastructure, but foreign operators, financiers and regional trading networks shape revenue flows and logistics priorities.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability near the Burkina Faso border require expanded security spending and create openings for external security, intelligence and development partners.

frictionVectors.title: Migration-for-finance bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European partners continue linking migration control, border enforcement, and financial support, limiting Tunisian negotiating autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported gas and electricity, while foreign-backed interconnectors and renewable projects shape its energy choices.

highlights: Oil corridor advances amid external pressure

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline project remains central to Uganda's resource strategy but faces international criticism, financing constraints, and pressure over environmental and social impacts.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and regional investors are increasingly important to transport, energy, and industrial infrastructure, creating long-term commercial and political leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western-linked mining firms dominate significant parts of copper production and processing, limiting Zambia's capture of downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked fiscal constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms improve financial stability but constrain public investment and bargaining power over strategic infrastructure and mining policy.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and platinum externalization
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms, especially Chinese investors, hold major positions in lithium and platinum projects, while Zimbabwe struggles to secure processing capacity and retain more value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions exposure, arrears, and limited access to conventional finance push the government toward concentrated partnerships with Chinese, Russian, and regional actors.
